li.a: The Second World War: Gondrand massacre
L'Italia Coloniale: L'eccidio del cantiere Gondrand a Mai Lhalà
I percorsi della storia: L'eccidio del cantiere Gondrand (Internet Archive copy)
Il Corno d'Africa, Gian Carlo Stella: I caduti del cantiere Gondrand di Mai Lahà (13 febbraio 1936)

content.p: In the early hours of 13 February 1936, a band of Ethiopian fighters reached a road-building camp just inside Ethiopia, near the village of Mai Lahlà, and overran it. The camp belonged to Gondrand, an Italian haulage and construction company, and most of the men sleeping there were Italian civilians. By the account most often repeated, 68 Italians and 17 Eritreans were killed, and many of the bodies were mutilated.

The attack came during Italy's invasion of Ethiopia. It has been remembered in two incompatible ways. In Italy it became the "eccidio", the slaughter, of unarmed labourers, and Fascist authorities gave it wide publicity. The Ethiopian commander who ordered it, Ras Imru, defended it as a lawful act of war against men working in a combat zone.
content.h2: A road-building camp at the edge of the front
content.p: Gondrand was building roads to link Adua with Eritrea. Its first site was near the village of Daro Taclè, where the firm was widening the road between Asmara and Adua. The location, in Ethiopian territory close to the Eritrean frontier, lay behind the front, according to the Italian accounts.

The researcher Gian Carlo Stella puts the workforce at 130, about three quarters of them Italian. Another Italian history page says the site housed a little fewer than a hundred Italian workers. The engineer Cesare Rocca ran the camp. His wife, Lidia Maffioli, was with him, and the deputy manager was Engineer Roberto Colloredo di Mels.

Two Italian accounts say the workers had no weapons because the camp lay in the rear and seemed safe, and that the headman of the neighbouring village of Mai Enda Baria had welcomed the work and asked to employ his village's unemployed men. One of them adds that Italian troops were stationed in the area but the camp was not visible to them. The same two accounts and the English-language page agree that the site held about 15 muskets, and one of the Italian accounts adds that there were no sentries. Ras Imru later argued that the workers were in an operational zone and armed with muskets, which made the attack legitimate.

Ras Imru's forces had slipped past the Italian positions during the night. The Italian-language accounts name the commander of the raiding party as Fitaurari Tesfai. The size of the force is not agreed: one account speaks of hundreds of armed men, and the medal citations written for the dead speak of 500 attackers. A short summary on the thesis site Tesionline describes a work crew of about a hundred men attacked and wiped out by one of Ras Imru's bands.

What happened inside the camp is reconstructed from what the first Italians found. According to Stella, nobody who could describe the fight survived, and the wording of the later medal citations should be read as presumption based on the scene the rescuers saw. Other Italian accounts, however, mention about twenty survivors. Among them was Lieutenant Clemente Ruggiero, who had stopped at the camp with a postal van that night. He escaped with a few others towards the Tacazzè river and was among the first to help the wounded. A workman, Giuseppe Fornara, got away in the confusion and carried word of the attack to the frontier posts.

Stella adds that a carabinieri vice-brigadier, Nicola Litto, and a driver for the government of Eritrea, Michele Porcelli, had arrived with the postal van. He says they stayed to defend the workers and were killed, and that Litto was awarded a silver medal for military valour. Rocca and his wife received bronze medals, and Colloredo di Mels a silver one, all after death. According to the priest Fra Ginepro, quoted by two Italian pages, the chief engineer fired every round from his revolver and was found lying with his face turned towards his wife. She was found shot with a pistol, probably, the account says, by her husband so that she would not be captured.

Two Italians were carried off as prisoners and later freed. Two Italian pages give their names as Alfredo Lusetti and Ernesto Zannoni, although Stella's list of the dead also includes an Alfredo Lusetti, and the pages do not reconcile the two.
content.h2: An explosion, and the Ethiopian dead
content.p: The Ethiopians did not leave unscathed. One English-language history page says that about 40 of them died, most when a store of gelignite at the camp exploded. Two Italian accounts give a larger figure, 68 losses, and likewise blame most of them on the accidental explosion of the camp's explosives store during the looting. Ras Imru said in July 1936 that the workers had defended themselves fiercely and inflicted heavy casualties.

A unit of the Italian 41st Regiment reached the camp a few hours afterwards. The first priest to arrive, Fra Ginepro, wrote that he saw about 70 bodies laid out in two rows behind the engineer, 18 of them castrated. The English-language history page, which files the event under atrocities, says 17 bodies had been castrated, despite an explicit order from Emperor Haile Selassie against mutilating the dead. The Italian foreign-affairs official Fulvio Suvich wrote to the League of Nations on 9 March 1936 about the savage treatment of the wounded and the dead. He listed castration, disembowelling, severed hands and the removal of eyes. These descriptions are Italian official and clerical testimony, and no Ethiopian or neutral examination of the bodies appears in the accounts consulted. The Ethiopian foreign minister was later shown photographs and had to concede that some Ethiopian soldiers had disobeyed the order against mutilation. He argued that it should be understood as a protest against Italian atrocities.

The dead were buried in a cemetery laid out beside the camp, and one photograph shows the same cemetery on the first anniversary of the attack. On 7 March 1936 Libyan Spahis of the Italian Second Army Corps found property taken from Rocca during a search of huts in the village of Adi Anfitò.

The usual figure, 68 Italians and 17 Eritreans, is accompanied in two Italian accounts by a further victim, an Abyssinian woman who worked as the camp's domestic servant. The English-language history page counts 130 workers, 68 Italians killed, 27 wounded and four missing, two of whom turned out to be prisoners.

Stella re-examined the numbers. The bronze plaque in the Gondrand head office in Milan carried 77 Italian names. By his count it left out the people who had died defending the workers. He added Litto and Porcelli, then searched the files of Italians who died in East Africa between 1936 and 1938, and found four more names. He set out a list of 83 Italians, noting that two workmen died of their wounds on 14 and 24 February. He also recorded three names on a semi-official list from the period that he could not confirm in any record and thought might be transcription errors. Stella says few of the local workers were killed, since most of them fled at the first assault. This is hard to reconcile with the figure of 17 Eritreans, and the pages do not explain the difference.

An Italian page records that Italian troops began a harsh reprisal against the people living around Mai Lahlà immediately afterwards. It says five passers-by were shot near the camp, and 18 people were killed in the village of Daro Taclè. Reports of brutal violence against the local population reached the Italian authorities every day, the page adds. Local chiefs and people thought to be guilty were hanged, and their bodies were left on the gallows for a long time as a warning, according to this account. Commanders also told Italians to keep their last cartridge for themselves, to avoid a brutal end if captured. The English-language history site puts it more broadly: after the incident, Italian soldiers killed many civilians in retaliatory murders.
content.h2: Propaganda, gas and a legal argument
content.p: Italian officials had generally told journalists not to write about Italian losses during the war. This case was different. The English-language history page says the story was deliberately promoted for its propaganda effect in presenting Ethiopians as barbarians. It also records that Italy's justification for using gas was the killing of the airman Tito Minniti and his copilot a few weeks before this event.

Ras Imru's own account, given in July 1936, was legal rather than moral. He said that he had himself ordered the attack. He said he considered it, and still considered it, a legitimate act of war, since the workers were in an operational zone and were armed with muskets. He contrasted this with the Ethiopian civilians who, he said, were attacked and decimated by Fascist aircraft and could not defend themselves.

The historian Luigi Goglia, quoted by an Italian colonial-history site, agreed with part of that. Ethiopians defending their country against aggression had somewhat more justification to make up for their weakness with ferocity, he wrote, and Ras Imru was right that the attack on the camp was a legitimate act of war and should be recognised as one. What followed once the Ethiopians entered the camp, in his view, belonged to the sad chapter of atrocities.

The names of the dead were put on the plaque in Milan. The remains of Cesare Rocca and his wife were brought back to Italy in the 1960s. The same colonial-history page says Rocca's brother Pietro then asked that an article be written to mark the dead and that no newspaper published it. It quotes the writer Dino Buzzati as saying that it would be a disgrace to dwell on the dead of an adventure war, who went to Africa to make their fortune.
